commit.message:
ci: keep codeql-action versions in lockstep and stop dependabot review failures (#205)

* ci: keep codeql-action versions in lockstep and stop dependabot review failures

Dependabot treats github/codeql-action's sub-actions as four independent
dependencies, so #201 bumped analyze to 4.37.4 while init and autobuild
stayed at 4.37.3. CodeQL rejects that skew and the analysis aborts with
"Loaded a configuration file for version '4.37.3', but running version
'4.37.4'".

Move all four refs (init, autobuild, analyze, upload-sarif) to 4.37.4
together, and add a dependabot group so future bumps arrive as one PR
rather than as separately-breaking ones. The version comments now carry
the full patch version so skew is visible in review.

Also guard the Claude review step on the OAuth token being present.
Dependabot-triggered runs read the Dependabot secret store rather than
the Actions one, where CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN is not set, so every
dependency PR failed the check before the review could start. The step
now skips cleanly instead; adding the secret to the Dependabot store
re-enables reviews with no further workflow change.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* ci: scope trivy token and skip SARIF upload on dependabot runs

The Trivy job ran without a permissions block, inheriting the repository
default of write. Narrow it to the contents:read plus security-events:write
that the SARIF upload actually needs.

That alone does not fix dependabot PRs: their GITHUB_TOKEN is capped
read-only regardless of what the workflow requests, so the upload fails
with "Resource not accessible by integration" and reds the check on every
dependency bump. Skip the upload for those runs. The scan still executes;
only the publish to the Security tab is skipped, and scheduled and
push runs continue to populate it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

---------

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commit.message:
ci: make the release image scan a real gate and scope workflow tokens (#206)

The trivy step in the release workflow was decorative. The preceding build
used push:false without load:true, so the image never entered the local
docker store and trivy resolved the reference from Docker Hub instead --
scanning the previously published release to decide whether to ship the
new one. Confirmed in the 1.4.8 run, where the scan reported at 20:39:14
and the image being released was pushed at 20:39:15. It also filtered to
UNKNOWN,LOW,MEDIUM, excluding the severities worth gating on, and set
exit-code 0 so it could never fail.

Load the built image, scan it by its version tag rather than :latest, and
split the step: HIGH and CRITICAL are reported for visibility, CRITICAL
fails the job before the push step runs.

Enabling the gate against the current base surfaced 19 fixable
HIGH/CRITICAL CVEs in openssl, musl and zlib, all inherited from the
frozen alpine:3.22.0 tag, which never receives updates while apk add
leaves already-installed packages untouched. Track the 3.22 branch (now
3.22.5, clean) and apk upgrade so the base cannot silently rot again.

Also add least-privilege permissions blocks to the release, lint and
sonar jobs, which were inheriting the repository default of write.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commit.message:
ci: run tests in Actions, align Go versions, tighten triggers and pins (#207)

go test appeared in no GitHub Actions workflow. The suite ran only in
CircleCI, so merge protection depended on a single external provider: if
it were disconnected or its token lapsed, PRs would go green with nothing
having run the tests and no sign of it in the Actions UI. Add a test job
mirroring the CircleCI invocation. It needs no secrets, as the live
provider tests skip unless their tokens are set and the backup directory
is created by the test preflight.

CircleCI ran cimg/go:1.24.0 while go.mod requires 1.25.1, so every build
silently downloaded a matching toolchain and would fail outright under
GOTOOLCHAIN=local. Track go.mod. The version 2 to 2.1 bump is left alone:
it is cosmetic here, cannot be validated without the CircleCI CLI, and
this is currently the only place the tests run.

The Trivy workflow triggered on watch/started, so starring the repository
launched a full scan; six of the last hundred runs came in that way. Its
unscoped push trigger also duplicated every pull_request run. Scope push
to main and drop the star trigger, leaving PR, main and weekly coverage
intact.

golangci-lint ran at "latest", letting an upstream release change the
result with no change here. Pin v2.13.0, the version the action last
resolved to and passed with. The lint workflow also matched branches with
'*', which does not match a slash, so pushes to dependabot/... and
fix/... never triggered it; use '**'. Finally, checkout now precedes
setup-go so module caching works and the Go version is read from go.mod
rather than a literal that drifts from it.

commit.message:
ci: derive the release tag from github.ref_name and fail the curl loudly (#212)

The release workflow triggers only on tag pushes, so github.ref is always
refs/tags/*, and the branch setting TAG=latest under a refs/heads/main
guard could never execute. Remove it.

The remaining step ran git describe --tags, which depends on the tag
object being present in a fetch-depth 1 checkout and would yield
<tag>-<n>-g<sha> if HEAD were ever not exactly on a tag, producing a
release asset URL that does not exist. github.ref_name is the tag name
directly. It resolves to 1.4.8 for refs/tags/1.4.8, matching the
--build-arg TAG=1.4.8 the last release actually used.

curl gains -f so a missing release asset fails at the download with a
clear HTTP error, rather than saving the 404 body to soba.tar.gz and
failing later inside tar with an unrelated message.

commit.message:
feat: publish the docker image for arm64 as well as amd64 (#213)

goreleaser has always produced soba_linux_arm64.tar.gz, but the Dockerfile
hardcoded the amd64 asset, so the published image was amd64 only. On arm64
hosts that means emulation where QEMU is configured and exec format error
where it is not, which rules out Graviton instances, most arm64 Kubernetes
nodes and small self-hosted boxes: plausible places to run a backup tool.

Substitute TARGETARCH, which buildx supplies per platform and whose values
match Go's naming and therefore the goreleaser archive names, and push a
manifest list so one tag serves both architectures.

The scan has to be restructured, because a multi-platform result cannot be
loaded into the docker image store. Build amd64 alone and load it for the
gate, then build and push both. The push build reuses the amd64 layers.
Scanning one architecture is sufficient here: both images resolve the same
alpine branch tag and install the same apk packages, and scanning an arm64
build directly returned an identical profile, 0 CRITICAL and 10 HIGH, all
Go stdlib from the release binary.

Selecting the docker-container driver also makes the existing load: true
load-bearing rather than incidental, since that driver does not write build
results to the local image store on its own.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commit.message:
chore: pin the build toolchain to go1.26.7 in go.mod (#214)

Which Go compiles a release was a property of whoever's shell ran
goreleaser rather than of the repository. On this machine that shell
exports GOROOT pointing at a downloaded go1.25.10 toolchain and puts its
bin directory ahead of the 1.26.7 install on PATH, so releases were built
with 1.25.10 and shipped ten fixable HIGH stdlib CVEs, all cleared in
1.25.13 and 1.26.4 through 1.26.6.

A toolchain directive moves that decision into go.mod. Verified in the
unmodified environment, GOROOT still exported: the build selects go1.26.7
and the resulting binary scans clean, 0 HIGH/CRITICAL against 10 before.
An older go on PATH switches correctly too, so goreleaser and CI both
pick it up without anyone remembering to unset anything.

The go directive stays at 1.25.1. It states the language version the
project supports, which is unchanged; the toolchain directive only says
what to build with.

One consequence: golangci-lint reads the toolchain directive to decide
its target version and refuses to run when built against something older,
so local runs need a golangci-lint built with go1.26.7 or newer. CI is
unaffected, pinning v2.13.0, which is built with go1.27.0.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

chore: switch to the gomodguard_v2 linter (#215)

superseded by a new major version under a new name:

  The linter 'gomodguard' is deprecated (since v2.12.0) due to: new major
  version. Replaced by gomodguard_v2.

The linter is enabled with no settings block, so there is nothing to
migrate. golangci-lint linters confirms gomodguard_v2 is enabled and the
old name disabled, and a full run reports 0 issues with the warning gone.
